title: Chapter VII
paragraphs: Cathy remained at Thrushcross Grange for five weeks, until Christmas. By then her ankle had healed completely and her manners were much improved. Our mistress visited her often and began her scheme of reform by using fine clothes and flattery to increase her self-respect. Cathy readily accepted both. So instead of a wild little savage without a hat leaping into the house and hugging us all breathless, a most dignified person descended from a handsome black pony, brown curls falling beneath a feathered beaver hat, a long cloth riding dress held up in both hands so she could sail inside. Hindley lifted her down, exclaiming delightedly, “Why, Cathy, what a beauty you've become! I hardly know you: you look like a lady now. Isabella Linton can't compare with her, can she, Frances?” “Isabella hasn't her natural gifts,” his wife replied, “but Cathy must take care not to grow wild again here. Ellen, help Miss Catherine take her things off—wait, dear, you'll spoil your curls—let me undo your hat.”

When I removed the riding dress, a magnificent plaid silk frock, white drawers and gleaming shoes appeared underneath. Her eyes shone with joy as the dogs bounded up to greet her, but she scarcely dared touch them for fear they would jump against her splendid clothes. She kissed me delicately: I was covered in flour from making the Christmas cake, so an embrace would never have done. Then she looked about for Heathcliff. Mr. and Mrs. Earnshaw watched their meeting anxiously, hoping it would show them how much chance they had of separating the two friends.

At first Heathcliff was not easy to find. If he had neglected himself and been neglected before Catherine went away, both had become ten times worse since. Nobody except me even troubled to call him dirty and tell him to wash once a week, and children his age seldom enjoy soap and water for its own sake. Consequently, quite apart from clothes worn for three months in mud and dust and thick, uncombed hair, his face and hands lay under a dismal cloud of grime. No wonder he hid behind the high-backed bench when such a bright, graceful young lady came in, instead of the untidy-haired double of himself he had expected. “Isn't Heathcliff here?” she asked, pulling off her gloves to reveal fingers wonderfully whitened by idleness and staying indoors.

“You may come out, Heathcliff,” Mr. Hindley called, enjoying his embarrassment and pleased to see what a forbidding young scoundrel he would have to present himself as. “Come and welcome Miss Catherine, like the rest of the servants.”

Catching sight of her hidden friend, Cathy flew to embrace him, planting seven or eight kisses on his cheek in a second. Then she stopped, drew back and burst out laughing. “Why, you look so black and cross! And so—so funny and grim! But that's because I've got used to Edgar and Isabella Linton. Well, Heathcliff, have you forgotten who I am?”
She had some cause to ask, for shame and pride together darkened his face and held him motionless.
“Give her your hand, Heathcliff,” Mr. Earnshaw said patronisingly. “You're allowed to, just this once.”
“I won't,” the boy said, at last recovering his voice. “I won't stand here and be laughed at. I won't put up with it!”
He would have escaped from the group, but Miss Cathy caught hold of him again.

“I didn't mean to laugh at you,” she said. “I couldn't help it. At least shake hands, Heathcliff! Why are you sulking? You only looked strange to me. Wash your face and brush your hair, and everything will be right: but you are so dirty!”
She looked anxiously at the dark fingers held in her own, then at her dress, afraid that contact with his clothes had done hers no good.
“You didn't have to touch me!” he retorted, following her gaze and pulling his hand away. “I'll be as dirty as I want. I like being dirty, and I'll stay dirty.”
With that he rushed headlong out of the room, to the master and mistress's amusement and Catherine's deep distress. She could not understand why her remarks had provoked such a display of temper.

After acting as lady's maid to the newcomer, putting my cakes in the oven, and lighting large, cheerful fires in the sitting room and kitchen for Christmas Eve, I prepared to sit down and entertain myself with carols, all alone. I ignored Joseph's declarations that the merry tunes I chose were little better than ordinary songs. He had retired to his room for private prayer, while Mr. and Mrs. Earnshaw occupied the young lady with various pretty trifles bought for her to give the little Lintons in thanks for their kindness. They had invited them to Wuthering Heights for the next day, and the invitation had been accepted on one condition: Mrs. Linton asked that her darlings be carefully kept away from that “naughty swearing boy.”

So I remained on my own. I breathed in the rich fragrance of warming spices and admired the shining kitchen equipment, the polished clock trimmed with holly, and the silver mugs set out on a tray to be filled with hot spiced ale for supper. Above all I admired the spotless cleanliness of my special pride, the thoroughly swept and scrubbed floor. After silently giving each object its deserved praise, I remembered how old Earnshaw used to come in when everything was tidy, call me a lively lass, and slip a shilling into my hand as a Christmas gift. That led me to remember his fondness for Heathcliff and his fear that the boy would be neglected once death took him away. Naturally I then thought of the poor lad's present situation, and my singing turned into tears. Soon, though, it struck me that trying to remedy some of his wrongs made more sense than weeping over them. I rose and went into the yard to find him. He was nearby, stroking the new pony's glossy coat in the stable and feeding the other animals as usual.

“Hurry, Heathcliff!” I said. “The kitchen's lovely and warm, and Joseph's upstairs. Come quickly and let me make you smart before Miss Cathy appears. Then you can have the hearth to yourselves and talk together as long as you like until bedtime.”
He went on working without even turning his head towards me.
“Come along—are you coming?” I persisted. “There's nearly a whole little cake for each of you, and getting you dressed will take half an hour.”

I waited five minutes, then left when he gave no answer. Catherine ate supper with her brother and sister-in-law; Joseph and I shared an unfriendly meal flavoured with rebukes from him and impudence from me. Heathcliff's cake and cheese stood on the table all night for the fairies. He contrived to keep working until nine, then went silently and gloomily to his room. Cathy stayed up late, with countless arrangements to make for welcoming her new friends. Once she came to the kitchen to speak to her old one, but he had gone. She stayed only to ask what was wrong with him, then returned. Next morning he got up early and, since it was a holiday, took his ill humour out onto the moors. He did not reappear until the family had left for church. Fasting and thinking seemed to have improved his mood. He hovered round me for a time, then gathered his courage and suddenly said, “Nelly, make me look respectable. I'm going to be good.”
“High time, Heathcliff,” I told him. “You _have_ upset Catherine: I dare say she wishes she'd never come home! You look as though you're jealous because people make more of her than they do of you.”
He could not comprehend _envying_ Catherine, but he understood perfectly well what it meant to hurt her.
“Did she say she was upset?” he asked, his face very grave.
“She cried when I said you'd gone off again this morning.”
“Well, _I_ cried yesterday evening,” he answered, “and I had more cause for tears than she did.”

“Yes, the cause was going to bed with an empty stomach and a proud heart,” I said. “Proud people make themselves a great deal of sorrow. But if you're ashamed of being touchy, remember to ask her forgiveness when she comes in. Go up and offer to kiss her, and say—you know best what to say. Only be wholehearted about it, instead of acting as though her fine dress has made her a stranger. Now, though there's dinner to prepare, I'll steal enough time to tidy you up until Edgar Linton looks like a little doll beside you—and he does. You're younger, but I'll wager you're taller and twice as wide in the shoulders. You could knock him over in a moment; don't you feel you could?”
For a moment Heathcliff's face lit up; then the cloud returned, and he sighed.

“But, Nelly, knocking him down twenty times wouldn't make him any less handsome, or me any more. I wish I had fair skin and light hair, dressed and behaved as well as he does, and had a chance to be as rich as he'll be!”

“And cried for your mamma at every little thing,” I added, “and shook if a country boy raised a fist at you, and stayed indoors all day because of a rain shower. Oh, Heathcliff, where's your spirit! Come to the mirror and I'll show you what to wish for. See those two lines between your eyes, those heavy eyebrows that dip in the middle instead of arching upwards, and those two black devils buried deep beneath them, never opening their windows boldly but lurking and gleaming like the devil's spies? Wish to smooth those sullen wrinkles away, and learn how. Lift your eyes openly and turn the devils into innocent, trusting angels, doubting and suspecting nothing, seeing friends wherever they don't know for certain there are enemies. Don't wear the look of a vicious mongrel that seems to think it deserves every kick it gets, yet hates the whole world as well as whoever kicked it for its suffering.”
“So you mean I should wish for Edgar Linton's big blue eyes and smooth forehead,” he replied. “I do, but that doesn't give me them.”

“A kind heart will help make your face handsome, my lad,” I went on, “even if you were completely black; a bad heart will make the prettiest face worse than ugly. Now we've finished washing, combing and sulking, don't you think you look rather handsome? I'll tell you: I do. You could pass for a prince in disguise. Who knows? Your father might have been Emperor of China, your mother an Indian queen, either rich enough to buy both Wuthering Heights and Thrushcross Grange with one week's income. Perhaps wicked sailors kidnapped you and brought you to England. In your place, I'd imagine a grand origin for myself, and the thought of who I really was would give me courage and dignity to endure a small farmer's tyranny!”

I chatted on in this way, and Heathcliff gradually stopped frowning and began to look quite agreeable. Suddenly a rumbling sound coming along the road and into the yard interrupted us. He ran to the window and I to the door, just in time to see the two Lintons climbing from the family carriage, bundled in cloaks and furs, while the Earnshaws dismounted from their horses: they often rode to church during winter. Catherine took a hand of each child, led them inside and placed them before the fire, which soon restored colour to their pale faces.

I urged my companion to hurry and show his good temper, and he willingly did so. But unfortunately, as he opened the door from the kitchen, Hindley opened it from the opposite side. They met, and the master, annoyed to see him clean and cheerful—or perhaps eager to keep his promise to Mrs. Linton—gave him a sudden shove backwards. He angrily ordered Joseph to “keep that fellow out of the room. Send him to the attic until dinner's finished. Leave him alone with the food for a minute and he'll be sticking his fingers in the tarts and stealing the fruit.”
“No, sir,” I could not help answering, “he won't touch a thing, he won't; and I suppose he's entitled to his share of the treats, like us.”

“He'll have his share of my hand if I catch him downstairs before dark,” Hindley shouted. “Get out, you vagabond! What! Trying to be a dandy, are you? Wait until I get hold of those elegant curls—see if I don't pull them a little longer!”
“They're quite long enough,” young Linton remarked, peering through the doorway. “I'm surprised they don't give him a headache. It's like a colt's mane hanging over his eyes!”

He ventured this without meaning to insult him, but Heathcliff's violent temper could not endure even apparent impudence from someone he seemed already to hate as a rival. He snatched up the first thing within reach, a tureen of hot apple sauce, and hurled it straight into Edgar's face and neck. Edgar immediately began a wail that brought Catherine and Isabella running. Mr. Earnshaw seized the offender and took him upstairs, where he undoubtedly applied a rough cure for the fit of anger: he returned red-faced and breathless. I fetched the dishcloth and spitefully scrubbed Edgar's mouth and nose, saying it served him right for interfering. His sister began crying to go home, while Cathy stood bewildered, blushing for everyone.

“You shouldn't have spoken to him!” she protested to young Linton. “He was already angry, and now you've ruined your visit, and he'll get beaten. I hate him being beaten! I can't eat my dinner. Why did you speak to him, Edgar?”
“I didn't,” the boy sobbed, escaping my hands and completing his cleanup with his fine linen handkerchief. “I promised mamma I wouldn't say a single word to him, and I didn't.”
“Well, stop crying,” Catherine answered scornfully. “You aren't dead. Don't cause any more trouble; my brother's coming. Be quiet! Hush, Isabella! Has anyone hurt _you?_”

“There now, children, back to your seats!” Hindley cried, bustling in. “That young brute has warmed me up nicely. Next time, Master Edgar, take the law into your own fists—it'll improve your appetite!”

The sight and smell of the feast restored the little party's composure. Hungry after their ride, they were easily comforted, since none of them had suffered any real harm. Mr. Earnshaw carved generous portions and the mistress cheered them with lively conversation. I stood behind her chair and was hurt to see Catherine, dry-eyed and apparently unconcerned, start cutting up the goose wing on her plate. “An unfeeling child,” I thought. “How easily she forgets her old playmate's suffering. I'd never have believed her so selfish.” She raised a mouthful towards her lips, then put it down. Her cheeks reddened and tears poured over them. She let her fork fall and quickly dived beneath the tablecloth to hide her feelings. I did not call her unfeeling for long: I could see that she was in purgatory all day, longing for a chance to be alone or to visit Heathcliff. The master had locked him in, as I discovered when I tried to bring him some food secretly.

That evening we danced. Cathy begged for him to be released, since Isabella Linton needed a partner; but her pleas failed and I was chosen to fill the gap. The excitement of dancing drove away our gloom, and the arrival of the Gimmerton band added to our pleasure. They were fifteen strong, with a trumpet, trombone, clarinets, bassoons, French horns and a bass viol, as well as singers. Every Christmas they visit all the respectable houses and collect contributions, and we considered hearing them a splendid treat. Once they had sung the usual carols, we asked for songs and part-songs. Mrs. Earnshaw loved music, so they gave us plenty.

Catherine loved it too, but said it sounded best from the top of the stairs and went up in the dark. I followed. Downstairs they closed the sitting-room door without noticing our absence, there were so many people inside. Instead of stopping at the head of the stairs, she climbed on to the attic where Heathcliff was locked up and called him. For a while he stubbornly refused to answer. She persisted and finally persuaded him to talk through the boards. I left the poor things undisturbed until I thought the songs would soon end and the singers be offered refreshments; then I climbed the ladder to warn her. Instead of finding her outside, I heard her speaking inside. The little monkey had crawled through one attic skylight, across the roof and into the other. I could hardly persuade her to come out again. When she did, Heathcliff came too, and she insisted I take him into the kitchen, since my fellow servant had gone to a neighbour's to escape our “devil's psalmody,” as he chose to call it. I told them I had no intention of encouraging their tricks; but since the prisoner had eaten nothing since yesterday's dinner, I would overlook his cheating Mr. Hindley this once. Down he went. I gave him a stool by the fire and offered plenty of good food, but he felt sick and ate little, and my attempts to amuse him were wasted. He rested his elbows on his knees and his chin in his hands, absorbed in silent thought. When I asked what he was thinking, he answered solemnly, “I'm working out how to pay Hindley back. I don't mind how long I wait, if I can do it in the end. I hope he doesn't die before I do!”
“Shame on you, Heathcliff!” I said. “Punishing the wicked is God's work; we ought to learn forgiveness.”
“No, God won't get the satisfaction I will,” he replied. “If only I knew the best way! Leave me alone to work it out. Thinking about that keeps me from feeling the pain.”

But, Mr. Lockwood, I forget that these stories can't entertain you. How foolish of me to chatter on so, with your gruel cold and you nodding towards bed! I could have given you Heathcliff's history, everything you need to know, in half a dozen words.

Breaking off in this way, the housekeeper stood and began putting her sewing aside. But I felt unable to leave the hearth and was very far from nodding. “Stay where you are, Mrs. Dean,” I cried. “Please stay another half-hour. You've done exactly right to tell the story at leisure. That's how I like it, and you must finish in the same fashion. Every person you've mentioned interests me, more or less.”
“It's just about to strike eleven, sir.”
“Never mind. I'm not used to going to bed in those long hours before midnight. One or two is early enough for someone who sleeps until ten.”
“You shouldn't stay in bed until ten. The finest part of the morning is over long before then. Anyone who hasn't finished half the day's work by ten risks leaving the other half undone.”
“Even so, Mrs. Dean, please sit down again, because tomorrow I mean to extend my night until the afternoon. I predict a stubborn cold for myself, at the very least.”
“I hope not, sir. Well, you'll have to let me skip about three years. During that time Mrs. Earnshaw—”

“No, no, I'll permit nothing of the kind! Do you know that mood when, sitting alone with a cat licking its kitten on the rug in front of you, you'd watch so intently that its neglecting one ear would seriously annoy you?”
“A very idle mood, I'd call that.”

“Quite the opposite: a tiresomely busy one. That's my mood now, so please continue in detail. I find that people in this district gain the same importance over townspeople that a spider in a dungeon has over a spider in a cottage, for their respective occupants. Yet this increased interest does not depend entirely on the observer's situation. They _do_ live more earnestly, more within themselves, with less attention to appearances, change and trivial things outside them. Here I could almost believe in love lasting a lifetime, though I never believed in any love lasting a year. One way of living is like sitting a hungry man down to a single dish, on which he can concentrate his whole appetite and do it justice; the other is like seating him at a table laid by French cooks. He may get just as much pleasure from the whole feast, but each dish means almost nothing to his attention or memory.”
“Oh! We're like people anywhere else once you know us,” Mrs. Dean observed, looking rather puzzled by my speech.

“Forgive me,” I replied, “but you, my good friend, are striking evidence against that claim. Apart from a few unimportant local expressions, you show none of the manners I am used to considering characteristic of your class. I'm certain you've thought much more than servants generally do. With fewer opportunities to waste your life on silly distractions, you've been obliged to develop your powers of reflection.”
Mrs. Dean gave a laugh.

“I do consider myself a sensible, steady sort of person,” she said. “Not precisely because I've lived among hills and watched the same faces and the same things happening all year round, but because I've had hard lessons that taught me wisdom. And I've read more than you might suppose, Mr. Lockwood. Except for those Greek and Latin books, and the French ones, you couldn't open a book in this library that I haven't looked into and learned something from. I can tell even those foreign books apart, which is as much as you can expect from a poor man's daughter. Still, if I'm to tell my tale like a proper gossip, I'd better continue. Instead of jumping three years, I'll be content to go to the following summer—the summer of 1778, nearly twenty-three years ago.”
